title: Getting started
text: Getting started Azox compiles .azox files into server-rendered HTML plus a small module that wires up signal bindings in the browser. Stable. Azox is at v1.1.0. The template syntax, the reactivity exports and the shape of the build output will not change without a 2.0. See limitations for what it deliberately does not do.

title: CLI reference
text: CLI reference The package on npm is azoxjs ; the command it installs is azox . Argument parsing is hand-written — there is no Commander or Yargs behind it.

title: CLI reference
heading: azox compile
text: Builds into .azox/build/ . With no flag it builds every page; --page takes a file name or a URL. The compiler parses the JavaScript it generated before writing it. A malformed expression fails the build, naming the page, rather than producing a file that breaks in the browser console.

title: CLI reference
heading: azox create
text: Creates a directory with a page, a second page to show routing, a component, a package.json and a .gitignore . It refuses to overwrite an existing directory.

title: CLI reference
heading: azox dev
text: Builds, serves at http://localhost:4321 , watches pages/ , and reloads the browser on save. If the port is taken it steps forward to the next free one rather than failing. When a page fails to compile, the browser is served the error instead of stale output, so a broken edit never looks like it silently did not apply. It recovers on its own once the page is fixed. Live reload uses Server-Sent Events rather than WebSockets. Reload is a one-way signal, so there is no handshake implementation to carry — which is how the dev server stays dependency-free.

title: CLI reference
heading: azox doctor
text: Checks the Node version, lists the route map, and fully resolves every page — including its components — so a broken reference surfaces before a build rather than during one. Exits non-zero when something is wrong.

title: CLI reference
heading: Commands
text: Command What it does azox create <name> Scaffold a new project azox dev Serve the project, rebuilding on every change azox compile Build every page azox doctor Check the toolchain and the project azox -v Print the version azox help List commands

title: CLI reference
heading: Using it as a library
text: The compiler is importable, and works without a filesystem — which is how the playground compiles in your browser.

title: Components
text: Components A component is a .azox file that declares what it accepts and renders markup. It is resolved at build time and inlined into its caller, so nothing about it exists at runtime.

title: Components
heading: Components can hold state
text: A component may declare signals of its own. Each use of it gets its own copy, so two <Counter /> tags hold two independent counts. Clicking one counter leaves the other alone. There is no component instance behind this — the compiler wraps each use in an ordinary JavaScript scope, so the two count declarations are simply two different local bindings. A component with no logic of its own is still inlined directly, with no wrapper at all. You only pay for a scope when you declare something that needs one.

title: Components
heading: Layouts and the document head
text: A component can carry a <head> block. Put the stylesheet, fonts and scripts every page needs in one shared component, and stop repeating them in each page. The blocks are merged: the component's lines come first, and the page's come after so a page has the last word. Identical lines appear once, and a component used twice contributes once — a stylesheet does not get linked repeatedly. A <title> or a <meta name="…"> that the page sets replaces the component's rather than joining it, since a document may hold only one of each. So a layout can set a sensible default title and each page override i

title: Components
heading: Lifting state up
text: When two components need to agree on a value, keep it in the page and pass it down as a prop, the way you would anywhere else.

title: Components
heading: Next

title: Components
heading: Props stay reactive
text: A prop passed as an expression keeps the caller's expression. In the example above, clicking the button updates the text inside the second card and nothing else — the component boundary changes nothing about how fine-grained the update is. A prop passed as a plain string compiles to static text with no effect attached at all, so constants cost nothing.

title: Components
heading: Slots
text: <slot /> is where the children nested inside the tag are placed.

title: Components
heading: Undeclared props are rejected
text: Passing something a component never declared is almost always a typo, and silently dropping it hides the mistake. The compiler stops instead:

title: Components
heading: Using one
text: Import it, then use it as a capitalised tag. Lowercase tags are always HTML elements, so the distinction is visible in the markup.

title: Components
heading: What the compiler produces
text: The markup is inlined, so the emitted code is what you would have written by hand. There is no component instance, no lifecycle, and nothing to reconcile. Rule Detail Naming Capitalised tag is a component, lowercase is HTML Importing A normal import statement, pointing at a .azox file Props Declared with props() ; undeclared ones are an error Missing prop Renders as undefined , not a crash Events on: attributes on a component are not treated as props Cycles Detected at build time, with the component named

title: Components
heading: Writing one
text: Declare props with props() , then use them in the markup.

title: Loops & conditionals
text: Loops & conditionals <each> renders a list and <if> picks a branch. Both are tags rather than a separate template language, so they nest inside your markup like anything else.

title: Loops & conditionals
heading: Branching
text: cond takes any expression. <else /> marks where the second branch begins.

title: Loops & conditionals
heading: How updates work
text: Each block marks its place in the DOM with a pair of comment nodes. When its source signal changes, the nodes between those markers are replaced — and nothing outside them is touched. The body is compiled once into a small builder function that is called per item, rather than being duplicated per entry. Everything else on the page, including other lists, is unaffected by an update here.

title: Loops & conditionals
heading: Keeping rows across a change
text: By default a change to the list rebuilds its contents. That is fine for display, but anything a row was holding — a count, focus, a scroll position — starts again. Give each row an identity with key , and rows survive: reordering moves them, removing one leaves the rest untouched, and adding one does not disturb what is already there. The key is an expression evaluated per row, so it can read the loop variable. Use something stable and unique to the row — a database id, not its position, since a position changes when the list does. A row that leaves has its effects released, and any onCleanup

title: Loops & conditionals
heading: Nesting
text: A conditional inside a loop sees the loop variable, and loops nest as deeply as you need.

title: Loops & conditionals

title: Loops & conditionals
heading: Objects
text: An empty list renders nothing, and so does a list that is null or undefined — useful while data is still loading.

title: Loops & conditionals
heading: Reference
text: Attribute On Meaning item={'{'}…{'}'} <each> The list to iterate. Required. as="name" <each> Names the current entry. Required. index="name" <each> Names the position, starting at 0. Optional. key={'{'}…{'}'} <each> Gives a row an identity so it survives a change. Optional. cond={'{'}…{'}'} <if> The expression to test. Required.

title: Loops & conditionals
heading: Rendering a list
text: item is the list, and as names the variable the body uses for each entry — the way a parameter names an argument.

title: Loops & conditionals
heading: Server rendering
text: Both are evaluated during the build, so a page arrives with its list already in the HTML rather than filling in once scripts run.

title: Deployment
text: Deployment A build is plain HTML, JavaScript and assets. There is no server to run, no adapter to install, and no rewrite rules to configure.

title: Deployment
heading: Any static host
text: The output has no special requirements. Upload it to S3, nginx, or anything else that serves files. Clean URLs work because every route is a directory with an index.html , which every static server already handles.

title: Deployment
heading: Checklist
text: Commit .gitignore with .azox/ in it — the build is generated Run azox doctor before deploying to catch broken references Use absolute paths ( /style.css ) for assets

title: Deployment
heading: Cloudflare Pages
text: Set the build command to npm run build and the output directory to .azox/build . No framework preset is needed.

title: Deployment
heading: GitHub Pages
text: On GitHub Pages a project site is served from a subpath ( /repo-name/ ), which breaks the absolute asset paths Azox emits. Use a custom domain, or a user site ( username.github.io ), to serve from the root. Add an empty public/.nojekyll . Without it GitHub runs Jekyll over the output, which drops any file or folder beginning with an underscore. For a custom domain, put the hostname in public/CNAME — both are copied to the build root like any other asset.

title: Deployment
heading: The build

title: Deployment
heading: Vercel
text: Import the repository, then set the output directory. Azox is not a framework Vercel detects, so choose Other as the preset.

title: Limitations
text: Limitations Azox is at v1.1.0. This page lists what it does not do, so you can decide whether it fits your project rather than finding out halfway through building one.

title: Limitations
heading: A layout is a component, not a route feature
text: A component can carry a <head> block, so one shared component holds the stylesheet, fonts and scripts every page needs — see Components . What there is no equivalent of is a layout that applies to a directory on its own: each page still imports the layout and wraps its content in it.

title: Limitations
heading: Expressions are evaluated during the build
text: Server rendering runs a page's <script> block through new Function . That is fine for project source you wrote, which is the same assumption any template engine's server step makes — but never point a build at .azox content submitted by someone else.

title: Limitations
heading: Hydration replaces the markup
text: On a page that has something to hydrate, the client module clears the server-rendered root and rebuilds it rather than adopting the existing nodes. Content is present before JavaScript runs, which is what matters for search engines and slow connections, but this is not true hydration. A page with no bindings and no listeners skips this entirely: it ships no JavaScript, so there is nothing to replace. That covers most pages of a content site — including nearly all of this one.

title: Limitations
heading: Lists rebuild unless you key them
text: A list without a key rebuilds its contents when the source changes, so anything a row was holding starts again. Adding key={'{'}item.id{'}'} keeps rows across reorders, removals and insertions. The default is deliberate — a list of plain text gains nothing from being keyed — but it does mean the behaviour differs depending on whether you remembered to add one.

title: Limitations
heading: No CSS pipeline
text: Files in public/ are copied as-is. Nothing is bundled, minified, scoped or hashed. There is no scoped-styles feature: a component's styles are global like any other CSS.

title: Limitations
heading: Routes are fixed at build time
text: Dynamic routes exist — a [slug].azox file builds one page per entry it declares — but the set of pages is decided when you build. There is no server rendering a URL on request, so a route that depends on something only known at request time is out of reach.

title: Limitations
heading: State does not survive navigation
text: Client-side routing exists, but each page starts fresh: navigating runs the new page's module from scratch, so its signals begin at their initial values. Nothing is carried across. There are also no view transitions — the swap is immediate rather than animated.

title: Limitations
heading: The index of a keyed row does not renumber
text: A keyed row is built once, so the index it was given is the position it was built at. Reordering the list moves the rows without renumbering them — the cost of keeping a row rather than rebuilding it. Use the index for a list that grows and shrinks at the end. When a list reorders and the position matters, read it from your own data instead.

title: Limitations
heading: What does work
text: The parts that exist are tested and behave predictably: signals, effects and computed values; components with props, slots and state of their own; loops and conditionals, nested to any depth; file-based routing; optional client-side navigation with prefetching; server rendering with escaping; the dev server with live reload; and a build that runs on any static host. Every one of these gaps is a deliberate stopping point rather than an oversight. Follow the repository to see what lands next.

title: Reactivity
text: Reactivity Azox has three primitives: signal , effect and computed . Everything reactive is built from them, and the whole runtime is about fifty lines.

title: Reactivity
heading: computed
text: A derived signal, recomputed when its sources change.

title: Reactivity
heading: effect
text: An effect runs immediately, and again whenever a signal it read has changed. Dependencies are collected while it runs, so nothing is declared by hand. Setting a signal to a value it already holds does nothing. Effects only re-run on an actual change.

title: Reactivity
heading: How this reaches the DOM
text: This is where Azox differs from a Virtual DOM framework. A binding in your markup compiles into an effect that closes over one specific DOM node. becomes, roughly: When count changes, that one effect runs and assigns to _el1.data . No component re-runs, no tree is rebuilt, and nothing is compared. The cost of an update is the cost of the assignment.

title: Reactivity
heading: Next
text: Template syntax — where bindings can appear Components — passing signals across boundaries

title: Reactivity
heading: onCleanup
text: Registers work to undo when the surrounding scope goes away — a timer to clear, a listener to remove, a subscription to close. A scope goes away when a row leaves a keyed list , or when an <if> takes the other branch. It also runs before an effect re-runs, so each run can undo the one before it. At the top level of a page there is nothing that ever removes the scope, so onCleanup never runs there. That is a page living as long as the document, not a failure. A cleanup that throws is reported to the console and the rest still run — a half-cleaned scope would leak whatever the others were holdin

title: Reactivity
heading: onMount
text: A script runs while its nodes are still being created, so anything that needs a real element has to wait. onMount runs once they are in the document.

title: Reactivity
heading: peek
text: peek() reads without subscribing. Use it when you need the current value but do not want the surrounding effect to re-run on change.

title: Reactivity
heading: signal
text: A signal holds a value and remembers who read it. Call it to read; call .set() to write. Reading is a function call rather than a property. That is what lets a signal know it was read: there is no proxy and no getter interception involved.

title: Reactivity
heading: What this means in practice
text: You might expect In Azox Component re-renders on state change Nothing re-renders; the bound node is written to Memoisation to avoid wasted renders Not needed — there are no wasted renders to avoid Dependency arrays Dependencies are tracked as the effect runs Keys to help a diff No diff exists Signals must be read inside markup or an effect to be reactive. Writing {'{'}count.peek(){'}'} , or copying the value into a plain variable first, produces a one-time read that never updates.

title: Client-side routing
text: Client-side routing Turn it on and links stop reloading the page: the next document is fetched, its markup swapped in, and its bindings started. Pages are prefetched when the pointer reaches a link, so a click usually has nothing left to wait for.

title: Client-side routing
heading: Cost
text: Around 2 KB, loaded once and shared by every page. It is loaded after the page's own module, so a page is interactive before navigation is enhanced.

title: Client-side routing
heading: Knowing when a page changed
text: A page's own module is re-run on every navigation, so its bindings work without you doing anything. A plain <script> that enhances the markup is different: it ran once when the site first loaded, and the nodes it worked on have just been replaced. The router announces each swap so such a script can run again. The event fires after the new markup is in place and after the page's module has run, so a listener always sees the finished page. event.detail holds url and from , which is enough to tell a section change from a move to another part of the site.

title: Client-side routing
heading: Links it leaves alone
text: A link is only intercepted when a plain client-side navigation is clearly what was meant. Cmd-click, Ctrl-click and middle-click are left alone too, so opening a link in a new tab keeps working.

title: Client-side routing
heading: Next
text: Routing — how files become URLs Deployment

title: Client-side routing
heading: Turning it on
text: Add "router": true to your project's package.json . It is off by default, because changing how every link behaves is not something a project should get without asking. Nothing else changes. Keep writing ordinary <a href="/about"> links — the router attaches itself to the ones it can handle.

title: Client-side routing
heading: What happens to your state
text: Each page starts fresh. Navigating runs the new page's module from scratch, so its signals begin at their initial values. Nothing is carried across a navigation. This is the honest consequence of pages being independent documents. If you need a value to survive navigation, put it somewhere that outlives the page — sessionStorage , or the URL itself.

title: Client-side routing
heading: What it does
text: Event Behaviour Pointer reaches a link That page is fetched and held, so the click is instant Click Markup swapped, title and meta tags updated, scrolled to the top Back / forward Swapped back, with the scroll position the browser remembered Anything unexpected Falls back to a full page load, so navigation always completes

title: Client-side routing
heading: Without JavaScript
text: Every page is server-rendered and every link is a real <a> . With the script blocked or still loading, the site navigates the ordinary way and nothing is missing. The router is an enhancement on top of something that already works.

title: Routing
text: Routing The layout of pages/ is the routing table. There is no router to configure and no route file to keep in sync.

title: Routing
heading: Building one page
text: By file name or by URL, whichever reads better:

title: Routing
heading: Files to URLs
text: File URL pages/index.azox / pages/about.azox /about pages/blog/index.azox /blog pages/blog/first-post.azox /blog/first-post pages/docs/guide/setup.azox /docs/guide/setup A file named index takes the name of its directory rather than adding a segment, so blog/index.azox is /blog and not /blog/index . Directories can nest as deeply as you like.

title: Routing
heading: Ignored files
text: Anything that is not a .azox file is skipped, as are dot-directories. Only pages become routes. Dynamic routes such as [slug].azox are not supported yet. Every route is a file that exists at build time. See limitations .

title: Routing
heading: Linking between pages
text: Plain <a> tags with absolute paths. There is no client-side router in this version, so each navigation is a real page load — which also means each page arrives as server-rendered HTML.

title: Routing
heading: Next
text: Styling & assets Deployment

title: Routing
heading: What the build emits
text: Each route becomes a directory containing an index.html . That is what makes clean URLs work everywhere: serving index.html for a directory is universal behaviour, so no rewrite rules are needed on any host. The runtime is copied once, at the build root, and every page imports it through a relative path matching its own depth.

title: Styling & assets
text: Styling & assets Azox has no CSS pipeline. Files in public/ are copied to the build root untouched, and a page links to them the way any HTML page would.

title: Styling & assets
heading: Applying classes
text: Attributes keep their HTML names — class , not className . Braces make one reactive.

title: Styling & assets
heading: Linking a stylesheet
text: Use a page's <head> block. Its contents are copied into the document head verbatim. Use absolute paths ( /style.css ) rather than relative ones. A page at /blog/post is served from its own directory, so a relative path would resolve differently there.

title: Styling & assets
heading: Next
text: CLI reference Deployment

title: Styling & assets
heading: Page titles
text: A <title> in the head block wins. Without one, the title falls back to the name in your package.json .

title: Styling & assets
heading: Scripts
text: A plain script for behaviour that is not part of any page's reactive state — analytics, or a global click handler — goes in public/ and is linked from the head. The head block is per page. There is no shared document layout in this version, so a stylesheet link is repeated in each page that needs it. Components cannot contribute to the head.

title: Styling & assets
heading: The public directory
text: A file keeps the same path in source and in the built site, so a link written during development is the link that ships.

title: Styling & assets
heading: What is not included
text: Azox does not bundle, minify, hash filenames, or process CSS. Files are served as written. If you need a build step for your styles, run it yourself and output into public/ .

title: Template syntax
text: Template syntax A .azox file is HTML with three additions: braces for expressions, on: for events, and optional <script> and <head> blocks. It is not JSX — attributes keep their HTML names, and there is no className .

title: Template syntax
heading: Attributes
text: Quoted values are static; braces make an attribute reactive. A reactive attribute gets its own effect, so it updates independently of everything else on the page.

title: Template syntax
heading: Events
text: Prefix any DOM event with on: . The expression is used as the listener directly. Handlers can contain object literals and nested braces — on:click={'{'}() => user.set({'{'} name: 'Ada' {'}'}){'}'} parses correctly.

title: Template syntax
heading: File structure
text: A page needs a single root element in its markup, the way a document has one <body> . Wrap siblings in a container.

title: Template syntax
heading: Importing data
text: A <script> block can import a .json file, for a constant you would rather not write out by hand in several places. The file is read once during the build. Server rendering evaluates against it, and the value is compiled into the page's module as a constant rather than imported — the file sits outside the build directory and is never deployed, so an import would fail in the browser. Only the properties your markup reads are included. Importing package.json for a version does not ship the rest of the file to every visitor. Importing a .js module is not supported. It would mean running your proje

title: Template syntax
heading: Interpolation
text: Braces evaluate an expression and insert the result as text. Values are escaped, so text that looks like markup is shown, not interpreted.

title: Template syntax
heading: It picks the right property and event
text: Written by hand these are easy to get wrong, and wrong quietly. Name the signal, do not call it: bind:value={'{'}draft{'}'} , not bind:value={'{'}draft(){'}'} . A binding has to write back, which a value cannot do — so the called form is rejected at build time rather than half working.

title: Template syntax
heading: Literal text
text: To show markup or braces as-is — a code sample, for instance — wrap it in <text> . Nothing inside is parsed as markup or interpolated. This documentation is written in Azox and uses it for every snippet.

title: Template syntax
heading: More than one root
text: A page or component may have several root elements. They are placed directly where the component is used, with nothing wrapped around them. This matters where the parent element restricts what may sit inside it: a <div> wrapper is invalid in a <ul> , a <dl> or a <tbody> .

title: Template syntax
heading: Next
text: Components — splitting a page up Routing — turning files into URLs

title: Template syntax
heading: Reference
text: Syntax Meaning {'{'}expr{'}'} Insert the value of an expression, escaped attr={'{'}expr{'}'} A reactive attribute attr="value" A static attribute on:event={'{'}fn{'}'} Attach a DOM event listener <Capitalised /> A component <slot /> Where a component places its children <text>…</text> Literal content, never parsed

title: Template syntax
heading: Two-way inputs
text: bind: keeps an element and a signal in step in both directions, so you do not write a value= and an on:input= that have to agree. The element follows the signal, and the signal follows the element. Setting the signal from anywhere else updates the input too.

title: Getting started
heading: Build for production
text: The output lands in .azox/build/ : That directory is a complete static site. Every route is a directory with an index.html , so clean URLs work on any host without rewrite rules. See deployment .

text: The dev server starts at http://localhost:4321 , rebuilds when you save, and reloads the browser. The npm package is azoxjs , but the command it installs is azox . The short name was already blocked on npm.

text: Node 18 or newer. Nothing else — Azox has no dependencies.

title: Getting started
heading: What you get
text: There is no configuration file. The folder layout is the configuration: pages become routes, and public/ is copied as-is.

title: Getting started
heading: Your first page
text: A page is markup, with an optional <script> block for state and an optional <head> block for document metadata. signal(0) creates a reactive value. Reading it as count() inside markup binds that spot in the DOM to it — and only that spot.
